and the human situation generally, serves as an occasion to explore the nature of poetic
creation and of creativity itself. The immediate precedents for S.’s poem are to be found in
Wordsworth’s apostrophes To a Sky-Lark, To the Cuckoo, O Nightingale! and The Green
Linnet (1807), and in Coleridge’s The Nightingale (1798): particular resemblances are
recorded in the notes. But the literary pedigree of such appropriations of a natural crea-
ture to poetic uses reaches back to the ancient Greek lyric. In SP lxv (July 1968) 677–93,
Parks C. Hunter, Jnr. noted important parallels between S.’s poem and the anacreontic
To the Cicada, one of the most familiar of the ancient songs in the manner of Anacreon
(b. c. 570 bce) and frequently translated as one of his ‘odes’. Mary alludes to both insect
and song in a letter of August 1819:
